findings.message: When `normalized` is empty (e.g. input is `''`, or consists only of characters stripped by the separator/trim replaces such as `'---'` or `'!!!'`), `truncated` is `''` and `truncated[0]` is `undefined`. Calling `.toLowerCase()` on `undefined` throws a TypeError.
findings.consequence: slugify('') or slugify('---') now throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'toLowerCase')` at runtime instead of returning '' as before this change, crashing any caller that previously relied on an empty-string result for non-alphanumeric input.
findings.recommendedAction: Guard the empty case before indexing, e.g. `return truncated.length === 0 ? truncated : truncated[0].toLowerCase() + truncated.slice(1);`, or reorder so the case transform only runs on a non-empty string.

findings.existingCode:
const truncated = normalized.slice(0, MAX_SLUG_LENGTH);
  return truncated[0].toLowerCase() + truncated.slice(1);
findings.message: Slicing `normalized` to `MAX_SLUG_LENGTH` happens after the separator-trim step, so truncation can land exactly on an internal `-` and expose it as a new trailing character; the changed return line does not re-trim it. For `slugify('a'.repeat(63) + ' b')`, `normalized` is `'a'.repeat(63) + '-b'` (65 chars); slicing to 64 yields `'a'.repeat(63) + '-'`, and the change's `truncated[0].toLowerCase() + truncated.slice(1)` returns that string unmodified (first char was already lowercase from the earlier `.toLowerCase()`), so the function returns a slug ending in `-` instead of a clean 63-character slug.
findings.consequence: The test added in this same change, `slugify.spec.ts:14-16` (`expect(slugify('a'.repeat(63) + ' b')).toBe('a'.repeat(63))`), fails against this implementation: the actual return value is `'a'.repeat(63) + '-'`, not `'a'.repeat(63)`. Any consumer relying on a truncated slug never ending in a separator (e.g. as a URL path segment or CSS id) gets a trailing `-` for reachable inputs whose separator falls at the truncation boundary.
findings.recommendedAction: Re-apply the trailing-separator trim after truncation, e.g. `return truncated.replace(/-+$/, '')` (guarding the empty-string case per R01-001), so truncation cannot expose a stray separator.
